### Problem: Engineer Artem {#sec-mat-p5-artem}

::: {.p-statement}
An $n \times m$ matrix holds integers $1 \le a_{ij} \le 10^9$. Two cells are adjacent when they share a side. For every cell you may either keep the value or increase it by exactly one. Output any resulting matrix $b$ (so $b_{ij} \in \{a_{ij}, a_{ij} + 1\}$) in which **no two adjacent cells are equal**. An answer always exists.

$1 \le t \le 10$, $1 \le n, m \le 100$. On `[[2,2],[3,2]]` one valid output is `[[2,3],[3,2]]`; outputs are not unique, and any valid one is accepted.

Source: [CF 1438C · Engineer Artem](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1438/C){.solved rating="2000"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Colour the grid like a chessboard by $(i + j) \bmod 2$; side-adjacent cells always have different colours. Make every value's **parity equal its cell's colour** — keep $a_{ij}$ if it already matches, otherwise add one — and adjacent cells then have different parities, so they can never be equal.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Search the choices.** Each cell has two options, so try all $2^{nm}$ choice vectors (in a backtracking order that checks the left and upper neighbour as it goes) until one has no equal neighbours. Correct, and exponential.
2. **Fix the parity by colour.** Set $b_{ij} = a_{ij}$ if $a_{ij} \equiv i + j \pmod 2$, else $a_{ij} + 1$. Each cell is decided alone, in $O(1)$, with no search.

**Why it works.** Moving one step to a side neighbour changes $i + j$ by exactly one, so it flips $(i+j) \bmod 2$ (@sec-mat-a6). After step 2 every $b_{ij}$ has parity $(i+j) \bmod 2$, so two adjacent cells have different parities and are different numbers. The "$+1$" is always allowed because it is the only change made, and it is exactly the change that fixes a wrong parity.
:::

::: {#fig-mat-p5-artem}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
ea_a = [[2, 2], [3, 2]]
ea_b = [[v if v % 2 == (i + j) % 2 else v + 1 for j, v in enumerate(r)] for i, r in enumerate(ea_a)]
assert ea_b == [[2, 3], [3, 2]]


def draw(ax, p):
    chk = {(i, j): ("indigo" if (i + j) % 2 == 0 else "amber") for i in range(2) for j in range(2)}
    V.grid(ax, p, [[str(v) for v in r] for r in ea_a], x=0.0, colors=chk)
    V.grid(ax, p, [[str(v) for v in r] for r in ea_b], x=3.6, colors=chk)
    V.arrow(ax, p, 2.2, 0.0, 3.4, 0.0)
    V.text(ax, p, 1.0, 1.5, "a", size=9, color="muted")
    V.text(ax, p, 4.6, 1.5, "b", size=9, color="muted")
    V.text(ax, p, 2.8, -1.8, "a: the two 2s on top clash", size=9, color="muted")
    V.text(ax, p, 2.8, -2.4, "b: even on blue, odd on amber", size=9, color="muted")
V.show(draw)
```

A $2 \times 2$ example. Blue cells have $i + j$ even, amber cells odd. Every value whose parity disagrees with its colour is raised by one, so `2 2 / 3 2` becomes `2 3 / 3 2`: only the top-right cell changes, blue cells are now even, amber cells odd, and no two side neighbours can be equal.

:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Search the choices

::: {.form-next}
Backtrack over the cells in row-major order, choosing $+0$ or $+1$ and rejecting a choice that equals the left or upper neighbour. It always finds an answer (one exists), but in the worst case it explores $2^{nm}$ branches — only usable on tiny grids, as an oracle.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def artem_brute(a):
    n, m = len(a), len(a[0])
    b = [[0] * m for _ in range(n)]

    def go(k):
        if k == n * m:
            return True
        i, j = divmod(k, m)
        for d in (0, 1):
            v = a[i][j] + d
            if (i and b[i - 1][j] == v) or (j and b[i][j - 1] == v):
                continue
            b[i][j] = v
            if go(k + 1):
                return True
        return False

    assert go(0)
    return b


def artem_ok(a, b):
    n, m = len(a), len(a[0])
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(m):
            if b[i][j] - a[i][j] not in (0, 1):
                return False
            if i + 1 < n and b[i][j] == b[i + 1][j]:
                return False
            if j + 1 < m and b[i][j] == b[i][j + 1]:
                return False
    return True


assert artem_ok([[2, 2], [3, 2]], artem_brute([[2, 2], [3, 2]]))
```

##### C++

```cpp
struct ArtemBrute {
    int n, m;
    vector<vector<long long>> a, b;
    bool go(int k) {
        if (k == n * m) return true;
        int i = k / m, j = k % m;
        for (int d = 0; d < 2; ++d) {
            long long v = a[i][j] + d;
            if ((i && b[i - 1][j] == v) || (j && b[i][j - 1] == v)) continue;
            b[i][j] = v;
            if (go(k + 1)) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
};
```
:::

#### Fix the parity by colour

::: {.form-next}
Decide each cell alone: add one exactly when $a_{ij} \bmod 2 \ne (i + j) \bmod 2$. No search, no neighbour checks, $O(nm)$. The checker from the previous form confirms every output on random grids.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def engineer_artem(a):
    return [[v + ((v + i + j) % 2) for j, v in enumerate(row)] for i, row in enumerate(a)]


assert engineer_artem([[2, 2], [3, 2]]) == [[2, 3], [3, 2]]
assert artem_ok([[2, 2], [3, 2]], engineer_artem([[2, 2], [3, 2]]))
for _ in range(300):
    n, m = random.randint(1, 5), random.randint(1, 5)
    a = [[random.randint(1, 4) for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(n)]
    assert artem_ok(a, engineer_artem(a))
    assert artem_ok(a, artem_brute(a))
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int t;
    if (!(cin >> t)) return 0;
    while (t--) {
        int n, m;
        cin >> n >> m;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
            for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j) {
                long long v;
                cin >> v;
                if ((v + i + j) % 2 != 0) ++v;     // make parity of v equal (i + j) mod 2
                cout << v << (j + 1 < m ? ' ' : '\n');
            }
        }
    }
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Search the choices**: up to $O(2^{nm})$ time in the worst case, $O(nm)$ memory. **Fix the parity by colour**: $O(nm)$ time, $O(1)$ extra memory beyond the output — every cell is read and written once.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 1$ or $m = 1$: the grid is a path, and the same colouring alternates along it.
- A grid that is already valid may still be changed by the rule (`[[1,2]]` becomes `[[2,3]]`); that is fine, because the task accepts any valid output, not the one with fewest changes.
- $a_{ij} = 10^9$ becomes at most $10^9 + 1$, which still fits in a 32-bit signed integer; `long long` in the listing is only for comfort.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Greedy left-to-right fixing.** Raising a cell only when it equals its left or upper neighbour can create a clash with a later neighbour that has no legal value left; the global parity rule never needs to look back.
- **Diagonal neighbours.** Only side neighbours count. Diagonal cells have the *same* colour, so the parity rule says nothing about them — and the problem does not ask.
:::

**Variants.** [CF 1520C · Not Adjacent Matrix](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1520/C){rating="1000"} is the constructive cousin: place $1..n^2$ so that side-adjacent numbers never differ by exactly one — a checkerboard of odd and even numbers does it, apart from tiny cases. [CF 1366C · Palindromic Paths](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1366/C){rating="1500"} uses the other face of $i + j$: every monotone path visits the anti-diagonal layers $i + j = 0, 1, 2, \dots$ in order, so layer $s$ must match layer $n + m - 2 - s$.
